newsitem.title: USA: Money Store sees benefit from credit rating.
newsitem.headline: Money Store sees benefit from credit rating.

text.p: Money Store Inc, which offers loans to consumers with blemished credit histories, expects to benefit from its investment-grade debt rating as it expands its business to other underserved markets.

"In the specialty finance sector, there really aren't many investment-grade companies. We think this is going to be one of the defining characteristics of the company going forward," said Marc Turtletaub, president and chief executive.
Standard & Poor's assigned a BBB investment-grade rating to the company at the end of last year.
The company completed a securitization program during the first quarter of 1997, and for the first time, publicly offered $300 million of senior notes in April.
"The rating had a profound effect economically for the company," Turtletaub said in an interview after a presentation at a Piper Jaffray investment conference in Minneapolis.

In addition to the cost savings, he expects the rating will ease the company's access to capital, fueling its growth. "Over time, we will be able to access capital markets in a more efficient way," he said.
The company is currently negotiating expansion of its existing $400 million credit line, which it intends to use for general corporate purposes, including paying off higher-interest debt.

Money Store is a 30-year-old non-prime lender providing home equity loans, commercial loans, government-guaranteed student loans and autombile loans, mostly for used cars. It has 227 branch offices in 50 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico. Founded in 1967, the Union, New Jersey-based company made its initial public stock offering in 1991.

The company was founded by Turtletaub's father, Alan Turtletaub, who is currently chairman. It initially provided second mortgage loans to New Jersey homeowners with checkered credit histories. It expanded over several years by offering loans to people seeking to consolidate their debts or to make home improvements. Student loans initially were made to foreign students; loans to dental students followed.

Mining an untapped asset, Turtletaub said the company was looking for products and services to serve the people whose loan applications were turned down by the company. Money Store, which advertises heavily on television, receives about two million telephone calls a year from potential customers.
Turtletaub said this "low-hanging fruit" holds potential for new business. "This is an enormous corporate asset that we are not fully utilizing," he said.

The company found a vehicle for geographic expansion with its May acquisition of Platform Home Loans Ltd, a British mortgage company. The non-prime market is "virtually wide open in the U.K.," he said.
"Over time, there is some good upside potential for us in the U.K. as well as providing diversification for us," he added.
At the end of the first quarter of 1997, Money Store serviced a total loan portfolio of $13.2 billion.
In 1996, Money Store reported earnings of $85.7 million, or $1.44 a share ($1.41 on a diluted basis) and revenues of $778.7 million.
Money Store shares rose one to 27-1/2 Wednesday.
